title: The Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10)
hook: she comes with hard questions and says "the half was not told me"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon prayed for the foreigner. Your line was hear the stranger too. Did you give a newcomer your full attention? Today a foreigner does arrive, and she isn't coming to pray. She's coming to test. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

A caravan comes up the road to Jerusalem: camels loaded with spices, gold and precious stones. At the head of it is the queen of Sheba. She has heard of Solomon's fame, and she doesn't take it on faith. The 1917 Jewish translation puts it bluntly: she came "to prove him with hard questions." She isn't here to admire. She's here to check. And by the end of her visit she'll say a line that turns her doubt inside out. Today's word is the queen herself.
screen: `A CARAVAN TO JERUSALEM.` → `SHE HEARD THE FAME.` → `SHE CAME TO TEST HIM.`

segments.voice: First Kings, chapter ten. The Hebrew word for her hard questions is chidot, riddles. It's the same word used for Samson's riddle in the book of Judges. So she comes with puzzles, the kind that test a mind. The text says she spoke with him of all that was in her heart, and Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was hidden from the king that he could not tell her. Then she looks around. The house he built. The food on his table. His servants and how they're dressed. The offerings he brings up. And she says this, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it; and, behold, the half was not told me." The half was not told. Look at how she learns. She doesn't settle for the reports. She travels to see. She brings her hardest questions, not her easiest. And when the reality is bigger than the rumor, she says so out loud, with no embarrassment about having doubted. She also blesses Solomon's God, and says God made him king to do justice and righteousness. Then she gives her gifts, receives his, and goes home to her own land. The text never gives her a name. Later traditions tell more stories about her; Kings tells only this visit. It's a short scene, and it holds a way of learning. Doubt enough to go and look. Ask what you actually want to know. And be honest when what you find is more than you were told.
screen: `CHIDOT: RIDDLES, HARD QUESTIONS.` · `ALL THAT WAS IN HER HEART.` · `SHE SAW IT WITH HER OWN EYES.` · `A QUEEN WITH NO NAME.` · then, large: `THE HALF WAS NOT TOLD ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one hard question. Settle, and breathe. What's a question you've been carrying and never asked out loud? About faith, your work, a relationship, the way the world is. Not the easy one. The real one. Let it form into words. Then think of someone, or a book, or a teacher, you could bring it to. The queen traveled a long road for her answers. You may only need to send a message. If you pray, you can bring the question there first. The bell holds the time.
The Queen of Sheba. She came to test a king with riddles, saw for herself, and said the half was not told her. Today's word.
Your line: the half was not told. Today, before you judge something by its reputation, go and see it for yourself. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Jews read the visit of the queen of Sheba in the book of Kings, and the same visit is told again in the second book of Chronicles.

original.note: Hebrew: a riddle. the queen came with chidot, riddles, to test Solomon.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich queen came to admire Solomon.
what it means: she came to test him, saw for herself, and said the reality was more than the reports.
what a scholar hears: chidot, her hard questions, is the word for riddles, the same as Samson's riddle in Judges 14.

notes: chidot (10:1) as the same word as Samson's chidah (Judges 14:12): lexical claim, please confirm.
'Later traditions tell more stories about her' is deliberately unspecific; no tradition is named.
Verses 10:2–5 are paraphrased (all that was in her heart; nothing hidden from the king; the house, table, servants, offerings).
Editor: replaced a stock line and cut 'good or bad', which the text does not say.
